metadata.title: Three Lectures on Complexity and Black Holes
title_lines: Three Lectures on Complexity and Black Holes
metadata.abstract: This is the written version of three lectures on complexity and black holes given at PiTP 2018 summer program entitled ”From Qubits to Spacetime.” The ﬁrst lecture describes the meaning of quantum complexity, the analogy between entropy and complexity, and the second law of complexity. Lecture two reviews the connection between the second law of complexity and the interior of black holes. I discuss how ﬁrewalls are related to periods of non-increasing complexity which typically only occur after an exponentially long time. The ﬁnal lecture is about the thermodynamics of complexity, and “uncomplexity” as a resource for doing computational work. I explain the remarkable power of “one clean qubit,” in both computational terms and in space-time terms. The lectures can also be found online at https://static.ias.edu/pitp/2018/ node/1796.html . arXiv:1810.11563v1 [hep-th] 27 Oct 2018

Standard circuit architecture. Note that in each step the gates all commute because they act on non-overlapping qubits
The auxiliary system: The evolution of the unitary operator U(t) can be thought of as the motion of a classical particle moving through the group space SU(2K)
Relative-C
Vertex with d = 8
Regular tree with degree 8, depth 2

Two views of the circuit tree. On the left is an abstract decision tree. The complexity of the unitary leaf grows linearly with the number of steps from the identity at the center. Relative complexity is proportional to the number of steps between leaves
Two paths collide on the same epsilon-ball
Regular tree with degree 3

Graph ceases being a tree and doubles back. Since a group-space is homogeneous the structure must look the same from every vertex. The shortest loops (girth of graph) is of order 4K. Thus the red loop is too short. The loops must look more like the blue loop
50-vertex, (almost) regular d = 4 expander. Generated by some AI optimization protocol

120 vertex, regular d = 4 Ramanujan-expander. Quoting Donetti, et al.: “Some remarks on its topological properties are in order. The average distance 3.714 is relatively small (i.e. one reaches any of the 120 nodes starting from any arbitrary origin in less than four steps, on average.” Note: log 12
Evolution of complexity with time. The ragged red curve is the evolution for a speciﬁc instance of an ensemble. The smooth curve is the ensemble average
The left panel shows a (red) trajectory beginning at the identity and proceeding outward along toward greater complexity

Penrose diagram for an AdS eternal black hole. The diagram is foliated by maximal slices. The darker blue portions of the slices represent the wormhole behind the horizons. The volume of the slices “bounces,” decreasing in the lower part of the diagram, and increasing in the upper part
One sided AdS black hole formed by collapse
One sided AdS black hole foliated by maximal slices. The dark portions of the slices represents the region behind the horizon, i.e., the bridge to nowhere
The grey areas are not covered by the maximal-slice foliation
Circuit for a precursor
Each infected (blue) qubit infects each each qubit that it interacts with. The epidemic grows until all qubits are infected
Uninfected gates cancel with their mirror images
size as a function of time

An initially super-Planckian shockwave will eventually separate from the Planckian region and fall into the singularity. This occurs just at the Eddington-Finkelstein time when the complexity stops decreasing
An intially super-Planckian shockwave will be “kicked” into the singularity by a single thermal quantum. The green region is the Plankian region
